title: EZEKIEL SAYS SODOM WAS PROUD, OVERFED, PROSPEROUS, AND NEGLECTED THE POOR—THEN MENTIONS ABOMINATIONS
paragraphs: EZEKIEL SAYS SODOM WAS PROUD, OVERFED, PROSPEROUS, AND NEGLECTED THE POOR—THEN MENTIONS ABOMINATIONS
We keep using Sodom to talk about everybody else’s sin. Ezekiel does something far more terrifying: he makes comfortable religious people look into the mirror.
There is a way to read the Bible that keeps you comfortably innocent.
You find the murderer and think, “Not me.”
You find the adulterer and think, “Not me.”
You find Sodom and think you already know exactly who God is talking about.
Then Ezekiel ruins the illusion.
Because when God tells His prophet to describe the sin of Sodom, He begins somewhere many modern readers do not expect.
Not with the word most people are waiting for.
With pride.
With abundance.
With comfortable living.
With people who had enough bread to fill their tables while the poor remained unsupported outside their doors.
Read the Hebrew slowly.
Not the version somebody summarized for you.
Not the slogan from your side of a cultural argument.
The text.
“הִנֵּה־זֶה הָיָה עֲוֹן סְדֹם אֲחוֹתֵךְ”
Hinneh-zeh hayah avon Sedom achotekh.
“Behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom, your sister…”
Then comes the indictment:
“גָּאוֹן שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם וְשַׁלְוַת הַשְׁקֵט”
Ga'on, siv'at-lechem, v'shalvat hashqet…
Pride.
Fullness of bread.
Prosperous, undisturbed ease.
And then:
“וְיַד־עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן לֹא הֶחֱזִיקָה”
V'yad ani v'evyon lo hecheziqah.
She did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.
That is Ezekiel 16:49.
And suddenly Sodom is no longer safely ancient.
It is uncomfortably close.
Because what if one of the signs of spiritual decay is not merely what a society does when it is desperate…
but what it becomes when it has plenty?
What if judgment should make us examine not only our sexuality, our morality, our entertainment, our addictions, and our secret sins…
but our pride?
Our abundance?
Our indifference?
Our ability to watch another human being suffer while convincing ourselves that it has nothing to do with us?
And before anyone uses Ezekiel 16:49 to erase everything else Scripture says about Sodom, keep reading.
Because verse 50 is still there.
“וַתִּגְבְּהֶינָה וַתַּעֲשֶׂינָה תוֹעֵבָה לְפָנָי”
Vattigbahenah vatta'asenah to'evah lefanai.
They became haughty and committed to'evah—abomination—before God.
Then God says He removed them.
That matters.
We do violence to Scripture when we pretend verse 49 does not exist.
We also do violence to Scripture when we pretend verse 50 does not exist.
Ezekiel gives us both.
Pride.
Abundance without compassion.
Ease without mercy.
Neglect of the poor.
Haughtiness.
Abomination before God.
Judgment.
The Bible does not need us to rescue it from the parts that make our tribe uncomfortable.
It needs to be heard.
And there is something even more disturbing about this chapter.
Ezekiel is not primarily preaching a sermon to ancient Sodom.
Sodom was already gone.
God is speaking to Jerusalem.
That changes everything.
Jerusalem—the covenant city.
Jerusalem—the city associated with worship.
Jerusalem—the people who possessed sacred history and religious identity.
God reaches into the memory of one of the most infamous cities in Scripture and effectively tells Jerusalem:
You are looking down on Sodom while becoming worse.
That should frighten every person who knows enough Christianity to condemn somebody else.
Because it is possible to possess religious vocabulary and still have a Sodom-shaped heart.
It is possible to defend biblical morality and be consumed with pride.
It is possible to sing worship songs while ignoring someone God has placed within reach.
It is possible to own several Bibles while refusing to forgive.
It is possible to argue about righteousness online while treating actual human beings with cruelty.
It is possible to identify everybody else’s abominations while carefully renaming your own.
Greed becomes “ambition.”
Pride becomes “knowing my worth.”
Bitterness becomes “boundaries.”
Gossip becomes “discernment.”
Indifference becomes “protecting my peace.”
Materialism becomes “God blessed me.”
And sometimes a person can become so skilled at spotting darkness outside himself that he no longer notices what has been growing inside him.
That is the trap.
Sodom becomes useful when Sodom is always somebody else.
Ezekiel refuses to let Jerusalem play that game.
And Jesus will not let us play it either.
Remember how He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He did not lower God's standard of holiness.
He raised the light high enough to expose everyone.
Jesus could speak fiercely about sin while moving compassionately toward sinners.
He could confront hypocrisy without becoming hypocritical.
He could call people to repentance while allowing broken people to come near Him.
He could touch lepers.
Eat with tax collectors.
Receive the rejected.
Welcome children.
Speak with people others despised.
And then He could turn toward religious men convinced of their righteousness and expose the graves hiding beneath polished appearances.
This is where Ezekiel becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you have never participated in the notorious sins for which Sodom is remembered.
But have you become proud?
Maybe nobody would call your lifestyle scandalous.
But when was the last time another person's suffering interrupted your comfort?
Maybe your refrigerator is full.
Your closet is full.
Your calendar is full.
Your shopping cart is full.
Your phone is full of Christian content.
But is your heart full of mercy?
That question is not Marxism.
It is not partisan politics.
It is not a fashionable social slogan.
It is biblical.
God repeatedly reveals His concern for the poor, the needy, the widow, the orphan, the stranger, and the oppressed throughout Scripture.
And yet there is another danger here.
Helping the poor does not purchase salvation.
Generosity cannot wash away sin.
Feeding a thousand hungry people cannot make an unrepentant heart righteous before a holy God.
Christianity is not salvation by philanthropy.
We are saved by the grace of God through faith, not because our charitable record impressed heaven.
That means Ezekiel's words should not drive us into self-salvation.
They should drive us toward repentance.
Toward Christ.
Because if we are courageous enough to let Ezekiel's mirror remain in front of us, eventually all our comparisons collapse.
“I am better than them” stops working.
“At least I never did that” stops working.
“I go to church” stops working.
“I know the Bible” stops working.
“I believe the right doctrines” cannot become a hiding place for an unrepentant heart.
Eventually there is just you…
God…
and the truth.
Maybe you have been proud.
Maybe success made you less dependent on God.
Maybe comfort made you numb.
Maybe you have walked past people you could have helped.
Maybe you have withheld mercy because you thought someone deserved their suffering.
Maybe you have condemned sexual sin while secretly entertaining lust.
Maybe you have defended marriage publicly while destroying your own family privately.
Maybe you have preached generosity and worshiped money.
Maybe you know how to lift your hands during worship but cannot open those same hands to someone in need.
Maybe your sin looks nothing like the person you have been condemning.
It is still sin.
And this is where the story could become unbearable.
Except Jesus enters it.
Not to tell us sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how much it matters.
The Son of God did not endure betrayal, scourging, humiliation, nails, blood, and death because sin was a minor character flaw.
At Calvary, holiness and mercy meet without either one being compromised.
Jesus does not call evil good.
He takes the judgment sinners deserve upon Himself.
The proud can be forgiven.
The greedy can be forgiven.
The sexually immoral can be forgiven.
The self-righteous can be forgiven.
The indifferent can be forgiven.
The hypocrite can be forgiven.
The religious performer can be forgiven.
The person who wasted years running from God can be forgiven.
The person carrying secrets nobody knows can be forgiven.
But grace is not God's permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus saves sinners and begins transforming them.
Grace does not merely cover our scandal.
Grace confronts it.
Cleanses it.
Breaks its chains.
And teaches us to walk differently.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God standing over a broken sinner saying, “You are disgusting. Stay away.”
The Gospel invitation is Christ calling sinners out of darkness and into life.
Come into the light.
Stop defending what is killing you.
Stop hiding.
Stop blaming.
Stop performing.
Stop comparing yourself with someone whose sins look worse than yours.
Bring the truth to Jesus.
The scandal you thought disqualified you may become the very place where His grace becomes impossible to deny.
This is why the message of Sodom cannot be reduced to one fashionable interpretation from either side.
Genesis matters.
Ezekiel matters.
Jesus' references to Sodom matter.
The whole counsel of Scripture matters.
Ezekiel 16:49 explicitly identifies Sodom's pride, abundance, ease, and failure to strengthen the poor and needy. Ezekiel 16:50 immediately adds haughtiness and “abomination” before God.
We should neither delete the social sins to protect our preferred moral argument nor delete the abominations to protect our preferred cultural argument.
Let God speak.
All of it.
Because perhaps the most dangerous Bible is the Bible we have edited until it can no longer correct us.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years thinking Christianity is mainly about finding the people God is angry with.
Then you met Jesus.
And discovered that the Gospel begins when you stop pointing long enough to confess:
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
That prayer changes things.
Not because the words are magical.
Because grace meets the person who finally stops pretending.
There are people reading this with sins they have never confessed.
People smiling in church photographs while their marriage is dying.
People sharing Scripture publicly while battling pornography privately.
People serving everybody else while becoming spiritually empty themselves.
People with money who are terrified of generosity.
People with almost nothing who are still more generous than those with ten times as much.
People angry at God.
People exhausted from hiding.
People who believe Jesus can forgive everybody except them.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The answer is not to become better at appearing Christian.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Repent.
Trust Him.
Receive the mercy you cannot manufacture.
Then let that mercy reshape the way you treat other people.
Let forgiven people become forgiving people.
Let recipients of mercy become merciful.
Let people who have received generosity from God become generous.
Let those rescued from darkness stop using truth as a weapon for feeling superior and start carrying truth like a lamp toward people who are still trying to find their way home.
And yes, sometimes that means your faith reaches your wallet.
Jesus spoke about money because money has an extraordinary ability to reveal allegiance.
Generosity is not how we buy God's favor.
It is one way a transformed heart can respond to grace.
Support your local church faithfully according to biblical conviction.
Help people in need.
Support trustworthy Gospel work.

Think of it as voluntary Gospel partnership—an offering of support, not a price for God's blessing and not a replacement for obedience to whatever biblical convictions and responsibilities you have concerning giving through your local church.
And there is something else we want believers serious about growing deeper in Jesus to know.
Not because information can replace Christ.
But because biblical nourishment matters.
Discipleship matters.
Truth matters.
And in an age when people consume endless hours of content that leaves their souls starving, we want to keep putting Christ-centered resources within reach.
That costs nothing.
Someone quietly losing a battle.
Someone hiding a secret.
Someone angry with Christianity because all they have ever encountered is condemnation without tears.
Someone prosperous on the outside and spiritually starving inside.
Someone who needs to discover that biblical holiness and biblical compassion were never enemies.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops hiding.
If this exposed something in you, comment, “Jesus, search my heart.”
If you are exhausted from pretending you are spiritually okay, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ is confronting and healing places you have kept hidden, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if you have been judging everybody else's darkness while God has been pointing toward something in your own heart…
“No more hiding.”
Then pray those words when nobody else is watching.
Because the goal is not comments.
The goal is Christ.
The goal is not viral outrage.
The goal is repentance.
The goal is not winning another argument about Sodom.
The goal is letting the God who spoke through Ezekiel search us.
Pride.
Fullness.
Ease.
Neglected suffering.
Haughtiness.
Abomination.
These are not merely archaeological remains from a ruined city.
They are warnings.
And warnings are mercy when there is still time to turn around.
Maybe that is why this passage feels so sharp.
We wanted Ezekiel to give us ammunition.
Instead, he handed us a mirror.
And standing behind that mirror is not a Savior waiting for an excuse to destroy the repentant.
There is Jesus.
Scarred hands.
A cross behind Him.
An empty tomb ahead.
And an invitation that sinners have been hearing for two thousand years:
Come.
Not after you repair yourself.
Come because you cannot.
Come with the pride.
Come with the greed.
Come with the sexual sin.
Come with the indifference.
Come with the hypocrisy.
Come with the secret browser history.
Come with the religious mask.
Come with the money you worshiped.
Come with the people you refused to forgive.
Come with the shame you thought you would carry into the grave.
Come to Jesus in repentance and faith.
He does not rewrite evil by pretending it was good.
He rewrites the sinner's future by forgiving, cleansing, redeeming, and transforming those who come to Him.
Sodom's story warns us what pride, abundance without mercy, haughtiness, and rebellion against God can become.
The cross tells us what God's mercy was willing to endure to rescue sinners.
So before you close this…
do not ask only what Sodom did.
Ask what Ezekiel is exposing in you.
Then ask the question that matters even more:
What will I do with Jesus now that I have seen it?
Because sometimes the person standing closest to judgment is the one so busy identifying everybody else's sin that he never notices grace calling his own name.
